summary: Describes a working implementation that lets applications directly use ATM services with the ST2+ stream protocol, covering several mixed internet and ATM setups. It is informational.

eli5.summary: This explains how a program that streams video could ask a special fast network to carry it directly, without going through extra layers.

questions: what is native atm support for st2+
how does st2+ work over atm
how do you map st2+ qos parameters to atm
what is the best signalling mechanism for st2+ over atm
subtitle: Run ST2+ connection-oriented streaming over ATM networks with guaranteed quality of service.

tldr.problem: Applications need bandwidth guarantees and quality of service for streaming, but ATM networks and the ST2+ streaming protocol use different signalling and resource models, making integration difficult.
tldr.mechanism: This document describes how to map ST2+ reservation requests to ATM virtual circuits, separating reservation signalling from data transmission and translating QoS parameters between the two systems.
tldr.outcome: Applications can use ST2+ to reserve bandwidth and guarantee quality of service directly over ATM, achieving both multicast capability and QoS guarantees in mixed ATM and Internet networks.

today: RFC 1946 is an informational document describing one working implementation of ST2+ over ATM. While ST2 saw use in real systems for video and multimedia, the broader integration of QoS-aware streaming with ATM was not widely adopted. Modern networks use MPLS and Diffserv for traffic engineering and QoS, rather than ST2+.

sections.title: The Need for Native ATM Streaming
sections.content:
ATM networks and the Internet have different architectural philosophies. The Internet uses connectionless, hop-by-hop routing; ATM uses connection-oriented circuits with built-in quality of service. However, neither IP over ATM (RFC 1577) nor LAN Emulation fully exploits ATM's QoS capabilities for application traffic.

The ST2 and ST2+ protocols (also called IPv5) are connection-oriented streaming protocols designed to carry real-time traffic with guaranteed bandwidth and quality of service. They work well alongside ordinary IP but are rarely used directly over ATM. This document proposes a framework for mapping ST2+ reservations directly to ATM circuits, enabling applications to use QoS guarantees transparently across mixed ATM and Internet networks.
sections.eli5: The Internet and ATM networks speak different languages about quality and guarantees. This explains how to let a streaming program use the best features of both at once.

sections.title: Implementation Challenges for ST2+ over ATM
sections.content:
Mapping ST2+ to ATM requires solving several challenges. Addressing is problematic: ST2+ uses IP addresses, but ATM uses different address formats (NSAP). The solution is to use existing ARP facilities from IP over ATM.

ATM signalling (Q.2931 and UNI 3.1) does not support some ST2+ features. Dynamic bandwidth changes are difficult—ATM circuits cannot be resized in-place, so a change requires tearing down and rebuilding the circuit. Multicast maps well to ATM multipoint circuits, but only for origin-initiated additions and removals. QoS parameters differ between ST2+ and ATM—packet rates, delays, and error rates must be translated.
sections.eli5: ST2+ and ATM use different words for addresses, can't both change bandwidth on the fly, and count quality of service differently. Solutions exist for all of these, but they need careful engineering.

sections.title: Reservation Signalling Mechanisms
sections.content:
The document describes four approaches to signalling reservations over ATM. Embedded signalling combines ST2+ and ATM signalling into Q.2931 SETUP and CONNECT messages, but this requires ATM signalling enhancements and works poorly for multicast. In-band signalling is the simplest: set up ATM circuits with the requested QoS, then send data over them. Data and signalling share bandwidth.

A dedicated signalling virtual circuit separates signalling from data, allowing the data to use multipoint circuits while keeping control traffic on dedicated point-to-point circuits. This is optimal but more complex. Finally, signalling over IP over ATM or LAN Emulation leverages existing mechanisms, avoiding ATM signalling extensions but losing some QoS accuracy because the signalling and data paths may differ.
sections.eli5: There are four ways to tell the ATM network what quality the traffic needs: mix it with the ATM setup messages, send it alongside the data, use separate circuits just for signalling, or piggy-back on regular IP.

sections.title: Translating QoS Between ST2+ and ATM
sections.content:
ST2+ specifies quality with parameters like desired message size, packet rate, maximum delay, and bit error rate. ATM uses different parameters: peak cell rate (PCR), maximum end-to-end transit delay, and quality class.

The translation is mechanical but must account for both overhead and fragmentation. The CPCS-SDU size (the maximum packet the AAL5 sublayer accepts) is the ST2+ message size plus headers. The peak cell rate is the packet rate divided by the ATM cell payload size (48 bytes), accounting for the AAL5 trailer. Accumulated delay must include fragmentation delays. The RFC provides formulas for all the key translations, allowing implementations to map ST2+ parameters to Q.2931 SETUP messages accurately.
sections.eli5: ST2+ counts quality in packets and delays; ATM counts it in cells and bit rates. The conversion requires knowing how big packets are, how fast they arrive, and how fragmentation delays them.

sections.title: Implementation Experience and Deployment
sections.content:
The author describes a working implementation using all four signalling approaches. The best option proved to be dedicated signalling virtual circuits with multipoint data circuits, which provides accurate QoS tracking while leveraging ATM multicast.

Real-world measurements showed that ST2+ over ATM delivered more than three times the throughput of raw IP, and the quality remained consistent even when multiple applications shared the network. By contrast, IP traffic over shared circuits showed increasing degradation. The key insight is that dedicated circuits for ST2+ traffic isolate it from best-effort IP contention.
sections.eli5: When they built it, they found that using separate circuits for signalling and data, and letting ATM handle the actual forwarding, was the cleanest solution. In tests, streaming over ST2+ was three times faster than ordinary IP.

sections.title: Status and Security
sections.content:
RFC 1946 is an informational document describing an implementation approach. The document notes that ST2 and ST2+ are connection-oriented and origin-controlled, which naturally supports better security properties than connectionless IP, though the RFC does not elaborate on security mechanisms.

The RFC also observes that while ST2 has seen real commercial deployment for videoconferencing and video-on-demand, ST2+ was released late and had no commercial implementations at the time of writing. The approach is general and would apply to other similar protocols designed to establish native circuits.
sections.eli5: This is an explanation of how someone did it, not a standard everyone must follow. The connection-oriented design is naturally safer than just throwing packets around, though this document is not about security in detail.

left.title: ST2+ Signalling
left.desc: Connection-oriented, hard state, origin controls multicast, supports dynamic changes.

right.title: ATM Q.2931 Signalling
right.desc: Circuit establishment, quality parameters, multipoint simplex only, no dynamic changes.
